strengths: The paper exposition is quite clear, striking a balance between the lingo of algebraic geometry and the context of the ICLR audience.

The empirical popularity of attention-based networks, and the relative lack of understanding on the properties of said architectures (with respect to fully connected and convolutional ones, as the authors point out in L51-53) sufficiently justifies the theoretical exploration presented in this submission.

The authors identify lightning self-attention as a fruitful compromise that is both (1) amenable to their algebraic-geometric analysis and (2) a reasonably realistic neural network module. I believe the presented implicit hierarchy of modules (single-layer lightning self-attention, deep lightning self-attention, single-layer normalized self-attention, deep normalized self-attention) can be of use in further theoretical analyses of attention networks.
The authors introduce a “virtual weights” parametrization which enables an elegant analysis of deep lightning self-attention networks.

The submission poses a conjecture on the fibers for deep normalized self-attention networks (under their virtual weights parametrization). This conjecture is theoretically validated in the case of a single layer and empirically tested for deep networks. The communication of this conjecture to the relevant communities within the context of the ICLR conference can be beneficial towards advancing on its resolution.

The contributions reveal interesting properties of the geometry of lightning attention models and provide a rigorous characterization of the resulting functional space. The results are well-described and relatively straight-forward to follow.
As far as I can tell (although I am no expert in algebraic geometry), the claims are clearly stated and the mathematics are correct.

The paper presents a novel and rigorous theoretical analysis of undoubtedly important topics, i.e., attention mechanisms. The authors use algebraic geometry to develop a solid theoretical understanding of the neuromanifold of neural networks using attention mechanisms. Although the analysis is offered in a simplified context, that is standard and inevitable for a rigorous theoretical analysis and does not reduce the importance of their contribution. I believe the introduction motivates the study quite well (though it could be improved). Understanding the dimension and the topology of the neuromanifold is a consequential result, as it relates to the learning dynamics of transformers in the overparameterized regime (as authors point out, e.g., lines 246-248), and it could enable a series of future studies. The paper could potentially provide foundational insights with a potentially wide range of applications in understanding the mathematical properties of attention mechanisms in deep learning (though, whether this is achieved or not is not fully clear, as I discuss under weaknesses).
Analysis of linear self-attention networks with tools from algebraic geometry.
weaknesses: The submission falls short of adequately examining the implications of its findings; the authors could have expanded more on the “so what?” question after reaching their core theoretical goals.

In L416-419, the authors describe the dimension of the neuromanifold (~8.2B) versus the crude parameter dimension (~8.6B) but do not attempt to prescribe how to exploit this information; they could have explored how this difference might be leveraged for more efficient parameterizations or indicate redundancies that could be pruned.

The authors do not present a tangible demonstration of the implications of the neuromanifold’s dimension on sample complexity, even in a simple experimental setting; a basic experiment varying data amounts could have provided a more concrete link to the theoretical claims.

The lack of non-linearities in the attention unit (particularly the lack of softmax) is a critical omission, as softmax ensures attention weights sum to one; without it, the behavior is altered and the analysis may not apply to real-world scenarios.

The lack of residual connections between layers raises concerns about relevance to practical deep transformer architectures because residuals mitigate vanishing gradients and aid information propagation.

The lack of element-wise multi-layer perceptrons between layers limits expressive power and makes it unclear whether the geometrical properties observed would generalize to more realistic transformers.
It is somewhat unclear what can be inferred about realistic models based on this theory, especially because the softmax results point to no parameter redundancy.
The ultimate goal of the theoretical results and their implications are poorly explained; the paper does not clarify implications for the wider community or future theoretical research.
The implications of the theoretical statements are often not discussed; for instance, the main result (Theorem 3.13) is presented without discussion of its implication.
Even when implications are discussed, the ultimate goal or consequences of those implications are not discussed.
The experiments lead to a conjecture, but the theoretical relevance for future work that could lead to empirically relevant applications is not discussed.

There are too many technical details leading to the proofs or sketch of the proofs of the results, which should be moved to the appendix; the paper would benefit from a more high-level discussion of intuition and implications.
There is almost no review of the literature; many recent works on theoretical understanding of transformers are not discussed, limiting motivation.
While the introduction motivates the paper, the abstract does not reflect this motivation and could be improved.
The purpose of the visualizations in figures 2 and 3 is unclear.
Line 297 introduces a re-parameterization without explaining why it is introduced; the authors should explain it closer to where it is introduced.
The summary of the proof of Theorem 3.13 could be moved to the appendix; it is crucial to discuss the implications of the theorem instead of explaining the proof in the main paper.
The presentation can be improved to be more accessible to ML researchers.
Computing intrinsic dimensions of the neuromanifolds does not offer a significantly better characterization of the function space's complexity than simply counting parameters.

The small difference between the number of parameters and the dimension of the neuromanifold raises questions about the practical utility of this analysis; it is unclear if this difference has implications for expressiveness or trainability, or if it is an artifact of the parameterization.
The relevance of the fiber of the parametrization, the boundary of the neuromanifold, and critical points of the parametrization map to the deep learning community is not well-established.
Most results lack a discussion of their implications for training or generalization of linear self-attention networks.
Corollary 3.5 statement is too vague to provide practical insights into training algorithm behavior or model properties.
The paper does not sufficiently connect these geometric properties to concrete aspects of training, such as convergence rates, generalization performance, or robustness to adversarial examples.
While the results may be of interest to the algebraic geometry community, the reviewer does not see it being well appreciated by the ML community in its current form.
